claims.text: Integrating high-throughput EML-DSC experiments with AIMD calibrated or augmented by classical MD or machine-learning potentials will enable accurate and efficient determination of melting properties across a broad range of high-entropy-alloy compositions.
The proposed integrated approach can determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
The CoCrFeMnNi system is a canonical high-entropy alloy.
Experiments will use containerless electromagnetic levitation melting coupled with high-resolution differential scanning calorimetry.
The atomic-scale simulations will combine AIMD with classical MD or machine-learning potentials to improve computational efficiency.
An inert or high-vacuum experimental environment will minimize contamination.
The experiments will use controlled heating rates of approximately 100 K/min and optical pyrometry for temperature measurement.
Running simulations at thermodynamic conditions corresponding to the experiments will ensure proper calibration.
The droplet's thermal-radiation signature, hydrodynamic oscillations, and DSC endothermic peaks can bridge experimentally measured latent heat to simulated atomic-level structural changes.
Electromagnetic levitation provides containerless and uniform heating.
Containerless, uniform EML heating reduces extrinsic effects on melting behavior.
DSC provides precise detection of the enthalpy change during melting.
AIMD provides atomic-level information about changes in liquid short-range order.
Cross-validation between macroscopic measurements and microscopic predictions systematically reduces the uncertainties of the individual techniques.
The combined approach will determine melting temperature with approximately 2% relative error across a variety of HEA compositions.
The combined approach will determine enthalpy and entropy of fusion with approximately 5% error across a variety of HEA compositions.
The approach will generate a comprehensive and quantitatively predictive thermodynamic-property database for high-entropy alloys.
Well-characterized binary and ternary alloys with known thermodynamic properties can be used to calibrate and validate the method before applying it broadly to HEAs.
At extreme compositions or conditions, complex atomic interactions may reduce the accuracy of current machine-learning potentials or classical MD models.
There may be a trade-off between computational efficiency and accuracy when classical MD or machine-learning potentials are used for multicomponent HEAs.
